summary: This unit teaches you to put fabricated parts together accurately and safely: reading the assembly drawing, checking and marking the parts, setting them out, holding them with clamps, magnets and jigs, and checking that the work is square, flat, level and plumb. You will join parts by tacking and welding, by bolting and by riveting, control distortion, then inspect the assembly against the drawing, finish it ready for the customer and keep the records.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423). A fabricator does not only weld: most of the skill is in making the parts go together in the right place, at the right angle and within the sizes on the drawing. This unit teaches you to **assemble fabricated components**: frames, brackets, gates, grills, handrails, shelves and stands made from steel sections and sheet.

In Jamaica, small fabrication shops make burglar bars, gates, grills, water-tank stands, handrails, shop fittings and trailer frames. A gate that is out of square will not swing or lock; burglar bars made too big will not fit the window; a handrail with sharp welds cuts hands. Careful assembly saves material, time and the shop's good name.
**Who it is for:** Welding Level 2 trainees who can already measure, cut and tack weld, and who are learning to build complete jobs from drawings.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Control the hazards of heavy parts, pinch points, sharp edges, hot work, grinding and drilling; lift as a team.
Read the assembly drawing, parts list and tolerances; check and mark every part; plan the assembly order and the holding tools.
Set out and hold the parts
Use a flat setting-out table, clamps, locking pliers, magnetic squares, packers and jigs to hold parts in position.
Check sizes from a datum, check square by the diagonals or the 3-4-5 rule, and check flat, level and plumb.
Fit parts with the right gaps, put misfits right properly, tack in a balanced order and correct the job before full welding.
Use tacking, clamping, balanced and back-step welding and the right size of weld to keep the job in shape.
Mark, punch and drill holes safely; fit bolts, washers and locking devices and tighten them correctly; set blind rivets; tap threads.
Check the job against the drawing and tolerances, deal with anything out of tolerance, remove sharp edges and spatter, and prime.
Work as a team and keep records
Agree the plan, call lifts and measurements clearly, report problems and record the work on the job card.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on planning, holding tools, measuring and checking, tacking, distortion, bolting, riveting, drilling, inspection, finishing and safety.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact trade terms and simple calculations) and essays in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: assembling and welding a rectangular frame from pre-cut square tube, checked for size, diagonals and flatness; and assembling a bolted and riveted wall shelf, checked for size, square and level.

blocks.note: Short-answer questions ask for exact words such as try square, magnetic square, assembly drawing, pilot hole, primer, tap and rivet gun, and for simple sums: a diagonal by the 3-4-5 rule, or the largest size a tolerance allows. Practise the sums in this kit.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Assembly work mixes heavy lifting, hand tools, power tools and hot work, often with several people round one job. Most injuries are to **hands, feet and backs**.

head: Hazard
What can happen
How you control it
rows: Back injuries from lifting heavy or awkward parts; crushed feet from dropped steel
Plan the lift and the route
Use enough people or a lifting aid
Lift with your legs, back straight, load close
Fingers trapped between parts, in clamps, under magnets or between a part and the table
Keep fingers clear when parts are brought together
Line up holes with a podger, never a finger
Cuts from sawn and sheared edges, burrs and sheet
Burns, arc flash, fumes and fire when tacking and welding
Sparks, flying chips, a burst disc, noise
Disc rated for the grinder and undamaged; guard on
Work spinning in the hand; hair, sleeves, gloves or rings caught in the drill; flying swarf
Work clamped, never held by hand
No gloves, loose sleeves or rings at the drill; long hair tied back
Swarf cleared with a brush after the drill stops
Leads, hoses, offcuts and tools on the floor
Run leads and hoses out of walkways
A part tips off the table or a frame falls over when a clamp is released

flow: Look at the load: how heavy, what shape, any sharp edges, where you can grip it
Plan the route: clear it, open doors, decide where the load will be put down
Get help or a lifting aid (trolley, stands, a hoist used only by trained people) if it is too heavy or awkward for one person
Agree the plan; one person **calls the lift** so everyone moves together
Feet apart, knees bent, back straight; grip firmly and lift with your **legs**, keeping the load close
Move without twisting your back: turn with your feet
Put the load down the same way, on the call, keeping fingers and toes clear

blocks.note: Do not lift more than you can manage safely. A long frame may not be very heavy, but it is awkward, it swings, and the far end can hit people or catch in doorways. Two people, or more, and a clear route.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Task
PPE
rows: Gloves, safety boots, overalls, safety glasses
Welding helmet with the right filter, gauntlets, flame-resistant clothing, safety glasses under the helmet
Face shield over safety glasses, gloves, hearing protection
Safety glasses; **no gloves** near the turning drill; sleeves fastened; hair tied back

blocks.note: Gloves protect you from sharp edges when handling steel, but they are dangerous at a pedestal drill: a glove caught by the drill pulls your hand in. Take gloves off before you drill.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Document
What it shows
rows: How all the parts fit together, with the overall sizes, the position of each part, the joints and the weld symbols
One part on its own, with every size needed to make it
Each part's number, name, quantity, material and size
The job number, the customer, what is to be done, the finish, and spaces to record the work and the checks

ul: Sizes on engineering drawings are in **millimetres** unless the drawing says otherwise.
A **datum** is the line, edge or face that sizes are measured from. Measure from the datum the drawing uses.
**Weld symbols** tell you the type of weld (a triangle means a fillet weld), its size, its length and which side of the joint it goes on. Your instructor will show you the symbols your drawings use.
If anything on the drawing is unclear, or two sizes do not agree, **ask** before you cut or weld.

blocks.p: No part can be made to exactly the size drawn. A **tolerance** says how far a size may vary and still pass. It is written after the size.

blocks.note: A size outside the tolerance is a **reject** until it is put right, even if it is "only a little out". Never send it out, hide it with paint or force it into place: report it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Always measure from one datum, not from one mark to the next. Small errors **add up** when each mark is measured from the one before. If you mark five holes 150 mm apart and your reading is 0.5 mm long each time, the fifth hole ends up 4 × 0.5 = **2 mm** out. Measured from the datum, each hole is never more than 0.5 mm out.

flow: Read the assembly drawing and parts list: sizes, angles, joints, weld symbols, tolerances and finish
Check every part against the parts list: count it, measure it, check it is square and deburred
**Mark** each part with its part number (paint marker or soapstone) and which way round it goes, so it goes in the right place
Plan the **assembly sequence**: which parts go together first (sub-assemblies), where the tacks go, which joints are welded, bolted or riveted, and how distortion will be controlled
Choose the tools and holding devices: clamps, magnetic squares, a jig, packers
Prepare a clean, flat, level setting-out table and mark out the frame lines on it

head: Example: a steel table frame
Assembly sequence
rows: Check and mark the legs, long rails and short rails against the parts list
Set out and tack the two end frames (two legs and a short rail each) flat on the table; check them square
Stand the end frames up and join them with the long rails, using clamps and magnetic squares; check square, level and plumb
Tack all joints, check every size and diagonal, correct, then weld in a balanced order

blocks.p: For work that must fit a building, such as burglar bars, grills and gates, **measure the opening on site** before you build. Openings are seldom perfectly square. Measure the width at the top, middle and bottom and the height at both sides and the middle, and check the diagonals. Make the job to suit the **smallest** sizes, less the fitting clearance, and record every measurement on a sketch of the opening.

sections.title: Measuring and checking: square, flat, level and plumb

head: Tool
Used for
rows: Long lengths and diagonals; a flexible steel blade that rolls into its case. Check the hook at the end is not bent.
A steel blade fixed at 90° to a thicker stock: marks and checks right angles at corners
Checks that work is level (horizontal) or plumb (vertical)
A weight on a string; hangs truly vertical, for checking posts and uprights
Checks that a surface or member is straight and flat
Marks hole centres so the drill does not wander

blocks.h: Checking that a frame is square

blocks.p: A rectangle is square (all its corners 90°) when its **two diagonals are equal**. Measure from corner to corner both ways, at the same points on each corner. If the diagonals are not equal, the frame is a parallelogram: push in on the corners at the ends of the **longer** diagonal until both read the same.
The diagonal of a rectangle can be worked out with **Pythagoras**: diagonal = √(length² + width²).

A triangle with sides in the ratio **3 : 4 : 5** always has a right angle between the 3 and 4 sides. To check or set out a large corner, measure 3 units along one side and 4 units along the other, and mark both. The distance between the marks must be 5 units. Any multiple works: 300, 400 and 500 mm; 900, 1 200 and 1 500 mm; 1 200, 1 600 and 2 000 mm. Use the largest you can, for accuracy.

blocks.note: If the 3-4-5 check is long, the corner is more than 90°; if it is short, the corner is less than 90°. Move the side until the check reads exactly.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Check
What it means
How to check
rows: All of the frame lies in one plane: no corner lifts
Lay it on the setting-out table and look for a corner that rocks or lifts; check members with a straight edge
Spirit level on the top member, in both directions
Spirit level on two faces at 90° to each other, or a plumb line

blocks.note: Check square, flat and size **after tacking** and again **after welding**, both while the job is clamped and after it is released. Welding can pull a frame out of shape even after it was perfect when tacked.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Setting out and holding the work

blocks.p: A flat, level steel table gives a true surface to build on, so the frame comes out flat and free of twist. Mark the outline or the main lines of the job on it with soapstone or chalk, and use stop blocks or angle iron as fences so parts sit in the same place every time. Keep the table clean of spatter and slag, which stop parts lying flat.

head: Tool
Used for
Points to watch
rows: Holding parts tightly together or to the table
Choose the right size; keep the screw clean of spatter
Quick clamping over a wider opening
Holding parts while fitting and tacking; quick to put on and take off
Set the grip before locking; can slip on a taper
Holds steel parts at 90° or 45° and frees your hands for tacking
Fingers can be trapped; keep it away from the arc, which it can make wander; it gets hot near the weld
A holder that sets each part in the same place every time, so many identical items can be made quickly and accurately
Check the first item from the jig against the drawing
Thin plates that fill a small gap or set a part to the right height
Use flat, clean packers; note where they go
Small, controlled adjustment of a part's position
Tap gently; do not force a misfit
Holds work while it is filed, sawn or drilled
Use soft jaws on finished surfaces

ul: Put clamps where they hold the part firmly but **do not get in the way of the weld**, so you can tack and weld without stopping to move them.
Tighten firmly, but not so hard that you bend thin tube or sheet.
Keep fingers out of pinch points as clamps close and as parts are brought together.
Clamps and magnets near the weld get hot: handle them with gloves.
A strong magnet near the arc can pull it to one side (arc blow). Move the magnet if the arc wanders.
Before you release a clamp, make sure the part is supported and will not fall.

flow: Mark the frame outline on the table with soapstone from a straight datum edge
Lay the side members on the lines; check each is the right part, the right way round
Set each corner with a magnetic square or a clamp and an engineer's square
Check the outside sizes against the drawing
Measure the diagonals and adjust until they are equal
Clamp the members to the table, clear of where the tacks will go

ul: Leave the gap the drawing or procedure gives. A small root gap lets the weld **penetrate** fully through the joint.
If parts do not line up, **find out why** first: a part cut too long, a burr, a bent member, or a mistake in setting out. Then adjust, re-cut or replace the part so it fits.
Never force parts together with a sledge hammer, and never fill a large gap with extra weld metal. Forcing leaves stresses and bends; a big gap filled with weld distorts the job and weakens it.
Use packers to set heights and fill small gaps, and wedges for small adjustments.

blocks.p: Tack welds hold the parts in place so the job can be checked and corrected before it is fully welded. Tacks must be small but **well fused**, so the full weld can melt them in.

flow: Tack one corner, then the corner **opposite** it, then the other two: a balanced order spreads the heat
Where possible, tack both sides of a joint
Check sizes, diagonals and flatness
If the frame is out, break the tack that holds it out, correct the frame, and re-tack
Check again before full welding

blocks.note: A tack that cracks is **ground out and made again**. Never weld over a cracked tack: the crack stays inside the weld.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Weld metal shrinks as it cools and pulls on the parts. A frame welded one whole corner at a time is pulled out of square towards the first corner. A long joint welded in one run bows. The more heat and weld metal, the more pull.

head: Method
How it helps
rows: Holds the job in shape while it cools; keep it clamped until the welds have cooled
Weld short runs on opposite corners or opposite sides in turn, so the pulls cancel, rather than finishing one corner at a time
On a long joint, weld short runs back towards the start, each ending where the last began
Weld short runs at spaced points along the joint, then fill the gaps
Set parts slightly out of line so the shrinking weld pulls them straight
Do not make welds bigger than the drawing asks; extra weld metal means extra shrinkage
Let a hot job cool in air before the next run; never quench it with water

blocks.note: After welding, check the job twice: while it is still clamped, and again after you release it. If it has moved, tell your instructor. Correcting distortion by heating and straightening is a job for someone trained to do it.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Mark the hole centres from the drawing (measured from the datum) with a rule, square and scriber
**Centre punch** each centre, so the drill point does not wander off the mark
Clamp the work in a machine vice or to the drill table: **never hold it by hand**
Drill a small **pilot hole** first, then open it out to full size
Use the speed on the drill's chart (smaller drills run faster) and cutting fluid on steel; ease the pressure as the drill breaks through
Stop the drill, then clear the swarf with a brush, never your fingers
**Deburr** both sides of the hole with a deburring tool or a larger drill turned by hand

blocks.note: At the pedestal drill: guard down, chuck key out before you start, no gloves, sleeves fastened, rings off, long hair tied back, safety glasses on. If the drill grabs the work, switch off at once; do not try to hold it.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Part
What it does
Points to know
rows: M10 × 50 means a metric thread, **10 mm** diameter, **50 mm** long. The numbers on the head (such as 8.8) show the strength grade: use the grade the drawing gives.
Screws onto the bolt to hold the joint
Same thread and grade as the bolt
The hole the bolt passes through
A little bigger than the bolt so it slides through: for an M10 bolt usually about 11 mm. The drawing gives the size.
Spreads the load and protects the surface from the nut
Spring washer, nylon-insert lock nut or lock nut
Stops the nut **shaking loose** where there is vibration
Use on gates, trailers, machinery and anything that moves or shakes

ul: Choose a bolt long enough that **a thread or two** shows past the nut, but not so long that it sticks out and snags.
Line up the holes with a **podger** (drift): a tapered bar that is pushed through both holes to bring them into line. Keep fingers out of the holes.
Fit the bolts with washers and run all the nuts up by hand first.
Tighten in a **criss-cross order**, in two or three stages, so the parts pull together evenly, the way wheel nuts are tightened.
Where the drawing gives a tightness (torque), use a **torque wrench** set to that figure. Never lengthen a spanner with a pipe.

blocks.p: When two different metals touch and get wet, especially with salt, one of them corrodes faster. In Jamaica's salty coastal air this happens quickly. Aluminium in contact with stainless steel or ordinary steel, for example, corrodes around the fastener.

ul: Use fasteners of the same metal as the parts where you can: aluminium rivets in aluminium sheet; galvanised bolts in galvanised steel.
Where different metals must be joined, keep them apart with **insulating washers and sleeves**, or a coat of paint or sealant between them.

blocks.p: A **blind rivet** (often called a pop rivet) is set from one side only. It is used to join sheet when you can reach only one side, and where welding would distort or burn through thin sheet, damage a painted or galvanised finish, or cannot join the two metals (such as aluminium to steel).

flow: Choose the rivet type, diameter and length from the maker's chart, to suit the total thickness of the sheets (the **grip**)
Mark the rivet positions evenly spaced, as the drawing shows, keeping each well in from the edge (a common guide is at least twice the rivet diameter)
Clamp the sheets together and drill the first hole to the size the rivet maker gives, just bigger than the rivet
Fit a rivet (or a temporary fastener) to hold the sheets, then drill and fit the rest
Push the rivet in, fit the **rivet gun** (hand riveter) over the stem, hold it square to the sheet and squeeze until the stem snaps off
Check each rivet head sits flat and tight

blocks.note: A loose or crooked rivet is drilled out: drill through the head with a drill the size of the rivet body, knock out the rest, and fit a new rivet. Do not make the hole bigger.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **tap** cuts a thread inside a hole, so a bolt or screw can be fitted without a nut. Drill the **tap drill** size first, which is smaller than the bolt, so there is metal left to cut the thread into.

ul: Taps come in sets: a **taper** tap to start, then a second (intermediate) and a **plug** tap to finish the thread to the bottom of the hole.
Hold the tap in a tap wrench, start it square to the hole, and use cutting fluid.
Turn it forward, then back a little every turn or so to break off the chips. If it binds, back off: a broken tap is very hard to remove.

blocks.p: When the assembly is complete, check it against the **drawing**, not against another trainee's job or by eye.

head: Check
How
rows: Overall sizes and the position of every part
Tape or rule from the datum, compared with the drawing sizes and tolerances
Diagonals equal, or an engineer's square at the corners
On the setting-out table, with a straight edge and a spirit level
Count them against the parts list; bolts tight with a thread or two showing; rivets set flat
Right size; no cracks, porosity, undercut or unfilled craters; spatter removed
No sharp edges, burrs or slag; moving parts work freely

blocks.h: When something is out of tolerance

flow: Do not hide it, force it, or send the job out
Mark the fault clearly (chalk or a tag) and stop work on that part
Tell your instructor or supervisor and agree the fix: re-set the part, re-make it, or accept it only if the person responsible for the job agrees in writing
Make the fix, then check it again
Record the fault, the fix and the final check on the job card or inspection sheet

ul: Remove all slag and spatter with a chipping hammer, scraper and wire brush.

Grind welds smooth with an **angle grinder** (a flap disc gives a smooth finish) where hands will touch them, such as **handrails**, gates and latches, so nobody is cut or snagged. Blend the weld into the parent metal **without cutting into it**: grinding a groove thins and weakens the member.
File or grind off burrs and sharp edges, and round off sharp corners.
Clean off rust, grease, oil and marking with a degreaser and wire brush, so the paint will stick.

**Prime** bare steel as soon as possible. In Jamaica's humid, salty air bare steel starts to rust within hours, and paint over rust soon flakes. **Primer** is the first coat: it protects the steel and helps the top coat stick.
Apply the top coat or other finish the job card asks for. Touch up damaged galvanising with the coating the instructor gives.
Check that hinges, latches and bolts work freely; fit any loose parts.

blocks.note: Grinding welds flush: face shield over safety glasses, gloves, hearing protection; the right disc for the grinder, undamaged, with the guard on; sparks pointed away from people and anything that burns.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Label the job with its job number.
Protect it so it is not scratched or bent before it reaches the customer: support long frames, pad the corners, never drag it.
Record on the job card what was done, the checks and their results, and who did them.

blocks.p: Assembly is often done by a team, with several people working on the same job at the same time. If people do not talk clearly, mistakes happen: two people cut the same part, a part is fitted the wrong way round, or someone starts welding while another person's hands are still in the frame.

head: Good practice
Why
rows: Agree the plan before starting: who does each task, in what order
No one doubles up work or misses a step
Everyone lifts and sets down together
Call out measurements and write them down, for example "diagonals 1 300 and 1 302"
The check is recorded and can be repeated
Warn others before you strike an arc or start grinding
Protects their eyes and stops them being startled
Report problems at once: a part out of tolerance, a faulty clamp, a damaged tool
Problems are fixed before they spoil the job or hurt someone
Hand over properly at the end of a shift
The next person knows exactly where the job is up to

ul: **Job card:** what was done, by whom, the time taken and the materials used.
**Ticked parts list:** every part checked and accounted for.
**Inspection sheet:** the sizes measured, the tolerances, the results and who checked them.
Records prove the job meets the drawing, help the next shift, and help find the cause if a problem comes up later.
Clean the setting-out table of spatter and soapstone marks.
Clean, check and put away clamps, magnets, squares and tools; report any that are damaged.
Sweep up offcuts, swarf and slag; put scrap in the scrap bin and sharp offcuts where nobody can be cut.
Coil leads and hoses and leave the area safe for the next class.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can name the hazards of assembly work and control them, and lift and move heavy parts as part of a team.
I can read an assembly drawing and parts list, and explain a tolerance such as 500 ±2.
I can check, measure and mark every part before assembly, and plan an assembly sequence.
I can explain why measurements are taken from one datum.
I can check a frame for square by its diagonals, work out a diagonal, and use the 3-4-5 rule.
I can check a job for flat, level and plumb.
I can set out parts on a setting-out table and hold them with clamps, locking pliers, magnetic squares, packers and jigs.
I can fit parts properly and deal with a misfit without forcing it.
I can tack in a balanced order, check and correct the job before welding, and weld it so distortion is small.
I can mark, punch, drill and deburr holes safely, and tap a thread.
I can make a bolted joint with the right washers and locking devices, tightened in a criss-cross order.
I can set blind rivets and say when rivets are better than welding.
I can prevent galvanic corrosion between different metals.
I can inspect an assembly against the drawing and deal correctly with anything out of tolerance.
I can finish a job ready for handover and keep the records.

terms: A drawing showing how all the parts fit together; also called a general arrangement (GA)
The order in which parts are fitted and joined
Welding short runs back towards the start to spread the heat
A rivet set from one side only; often called a pop rivet
A punch that marks a hole centre so the drill does not wander
A hole a little bigger than the bolt, so the bolt passes through
The line, edge or face that all measurements start from
Measuring corner to corner both ways; equal diagonals mean a rectangle is square
A job pulled out of shape by welds shrinking as they cool
Corrosion of one metal when two different metals touch in damp or salty conditions
A holder that sets each part in the same place every time
A magnet with angled faces that holds steel parts at 90° or 45°
A thin plate that fills a small gap or sets a height
A small hole drilled first to guide a larger drill
A tapered bar used to line up bolt holes
The first coat of paint on bare steel, to protect it and help the top coat stick
The hand tool that sets (pulls) a blind rivet
A flat, level table on which a job is marked out and assembled
A split washer that stops a nut shaking loose
A small weld that holds parts in place before full welding
A tool that cuts a thread inside a drilled hole
The drill size used before tapping, smaller than the bolt
A triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 units has a right angle
How far a size may vary from the drawing and still pass
A wrench that tightens a bolt to a set tightness
A steel blade fixed at 90° to a stock, used to mark and check right angles

c1.title: Canteen table frames in Brown's Town
c1.text: A group of trainees in Brown's Town, St Ann, is making rectangular frames, 1 200 mm × 500 mm, from 40 mm square tube for a school canteen. The drawing allows ±2 mm on the outside sizes, and the diagonals must be within 3 mm of each other. After the first frame is tacked on the setting-out table, the diagonals read 1 304 mm and 1 297 mm, and one corner lifts about 4 mm off the table. Jordan wants to weld each corner fully, one at a time, to save time.

c2.title: Burglar bars for a house in Port Maria
c2.text: Devon is measuring a bedroom window in Port Maria, St Mary, for burglar bars that will fit inside the opening. He measures the width as 1 210 mm at the top, 1 205 mm in the middle and 1 198 mm at the bottom. The height is 1 500 mm on the left and 1 504 mm on the right. His helper suggests building the frame 1 210 mm wide "so it covers the whole window".

c3.title: A bolted sign bracket in Half Way Tree
c3.text: At a shop in Half Way Tree, St Andrew, Kimani is making a steel bracket to hold a sign at a plaza. The drawing calls for four M12 × 50 bolts through the bracket's base plate, and for an M12 tapped hole in a 15 mm thick boss on the bracket for a lifting eye. Kimani has drilled the base-plate holes at 12 mm.

c4.title: Aluminium sign panels for a hotel in Negril
c4.text: Shanelle's team is fixing 1.5 mm aluminium sheet panels to an aluminium angle frame for a hotel sign in Negril, near the sea, using 4.8 mm blind rivets. The store only has steel rivets in stock. The drawing shows the rivets in a line close to the edge of the sheet. On the first panel, one rivet spins loose in its hole after setting.

c5.title: Finishing a staircase handrail in Hayes
c5.text: In Hayes, Clarendon, Marlon and Toni-Ann have welded a 3 m steel handrail section for a church staircase. It must be moved from the welding bay, through a narrow doorway, to the finishing area. The welds on the rail are rough, with spatter around them. The rail will be ground, cleaned and painted before it is fitted.

questions.q: If the frame were perfectly square, what should each diagonal measure?
questions.why: Diagonal = √(1 200² + 500²) = √(1 440 000 + 250 000) = √1 690 000 = 1 300 mm. Adding the two sides (1 700 mm) is a common mistake.

questions.q: The diagonals read 1 304 mm and 1 297 mm. How is the frame brought square?
o: Push in on the corners at the ends of the 1 304 mm diagonal
Push in on the corners at the ends of the 1 297 mm diagonal
Cut 7 mm off one of the long sides and tack it again
Add extra tacks on the long sides until the readings agree
questions.why: A frame out of square is a parallelogram: one diagonal is too long. Pushing in along the longer diagonal (after freeing the tacks that hold it) shortens it and lengthens the other until both read about 1 300 mm.

questions.q: One corner of the tacked frame lifts about 4 mm off the table. What does this show?
o: The frame is square, as long as the diagonals agree
The tube was cut 4 mm too long at that corner
The table is too small for a frame of this size
The frame is twisted and is not flat
questions.why: A frame that is flat lies with all four corners on the table. A corner that lifts or rocks shows twist, which must be corrected before welding; equal diagonals alone do not prove a frame is flat.

questions.q: Instead of welding each corner fully, one at a time, how should the frame be welded?
o: Weld the two long sides first, then both short sides
Weld all four corners fully at once with high current
Weld short runs on opposite corners in turn
Weld one corner fully, then check, then the next
questions.why: Welding one corner fully pulls the frame towards it. Short runs on opposite corners in turn let the shrinkage on one side balance the other, with the frame kept clamped to the table.

questions.q: Why did Devon measure the width at the top, middle and bottom?
o: To find the average width and build the frame to it
To find the largest width, so the bars fill the opening
Openings are rarely square, so he must find the smallest
To check that his tape measure reads the same each time
questions.why: Window and door openings are rarely perfectly square. A frame that fits inside must suit the smallest width and height, less a fitting clearance; the average or the largest will not go in.

questions.q: What width should the burglar-bar frame be made?
o: 1 210 mm, so it covers the whole width of the window
1 205 mm, the width measured across the middle
1 204 mm, the average of the three widths
A little under 1 198 mm, to allow fitting clearance
questions.why: A frame that fits inside the opening must pass through its narrowest point, 1 198 mm at the bottom, with a small clearance so it can be fitted and fixed.

questions.q: How should Devon record his site measurements?
o: On a sketch of the opening, showing where each size was taken
In his memory, as there are only five sizes to remember
As one width and one height, the largest of each that he found
On the wall beside the window, in pencil, for the fitters
questions.why: A sketch with every size, and where it was taken, lets the shop build to the right sizes and lets anyone check the work later. Writing down only one width loses the information that the opening is out of square.

questions.q: What is wrong with drilling the base-plate holes at 12 mm for M12 bolts?
o: Nothing: a 12 mm hole is right for a 12 mm bolt
There is no clearance, so the bolts will not pass
The holes are far too big for M12 bolts to grip
M12 bolts need holes of 10.2 mm to be strong enough
questions.why: A bolt passes through a clearance hole a little bigger than its diameter (often about 13–14 mm for M12; the drawing gives the size). A 12 mm hole leaves no room, so the bolts jam. 10.2 mm is the tap drill size, not a clearance hole.

questions.q: What does "M12 × 50" on the drawing tell Kimani about the bolts?
o: A metric thread, 12 mm in diameter and 50 mm long
12 bolts, each needing a 50 mm hole through the plate
A 12 mm long bolt that takes a 50 mm wide nut
A thread with 12 turns in every 50 mm of length
questions.why: M means a metric thread; 12 is the diameter in millimetres and 50 the length. The strength grade is marked on the bolt head.

questions.q: Which drill size should Kimani use before tapping the M12 hole in the boss?
o: 12.0 mm, the same as the bolt
13.0 mm, a clearance size
8.5 mm, as for an M10 thread
10.2 mm, the M12 tap drill
questions.why: The tap drill is smaller than the bolt, leaving metal for the tap to cut the thread into. For M12 coarse thread it is 10.2 mm; 8.5 mm is for M10.

questions.q: Which rivets should Shanelle's team use for the aluminium panels near the sea?
o: Steel rivets, because they are stronger than aluminium
Aluminium rivets, to suit the aluminium sheet and frame
Any rivets at all, as long as the heads are painted
Steel rivets, with extra rivets added to share the load
questions.why: Steel rivets in aluminium sheet in salty, damp air set up galvanic corrosion, and the aluminium round each rivet corrodes. Fasteners of the same metal as the parts avoid this.

questions.q: How far in from the sheet edge should the rivets go?
o: As close to the edge as possible, so they are hidden
Far enough that the rivet heads overlap the edge
Exactly half the rivet diameter in from the edge
At least about twice the rivet diameter, or as drawn
questions.why: Rivets too close to the edge tear out of the sheet. A common guide is at least twice the rivet diameter (about 10 mm for a 4.8 mm rivet), unless the drawing gives a size.

questions.q: How should the loose rivet be dealt with?
o: Drill it out with a rivet-sized drill and fit a new one
Squeeze it again with the rivet gun until it grips tightly in the hole
Fill round the rivet with sealant so that it can no longer spin
Drill the hole larger and fit a thicker rivet in its place
questions.why: A loose rivet is drilled out through its head with a drill of the rivet's own size, so the hole is not enlarged, and a new rivet of the right grip is fitted.

questions.q: Why are blind rivets used for these panels rather than welding?
o: Rivets are always stronger than any weld made on sheet
Welding cannot be done on any metal used near the sea
Welding would distort or burn through thin aluminium
Rivets need no holes, so the sheet stays fully watertight
questions.why: Thin sheet, especially aluminium, distorts or burns through easily when welded, and welding spoils a finished surface. Blind rivets join it cold, from one side.

questions.q: Before the 3 m rail is lifted, what should Marlon and Toni-Ann do?
o: Agree the route through the doorway and clear it first
Lift it quickly and work out the turn at the door
Drag one end along the floor so only one person is needed
Stand it on end and walk it through the door alone
questions.why: Long items are awkward even when they are not heavy: they swing and catch in doorways. Plan and clear the route, agree how to turn, and have one person call the lift.

questions.q: How far should the welds on the handrail be ground?
o: Down into the rail, so no trace of the weld can be seen
Only the spatter removed, leaving the weld rough
Flush and smooth, without cutting into the rail
Not at all, because the paint will cover the welds
questions.why: Handrail welds are ground smooth so they cannot cut or snag hands, but grinding into the rail thins and weakens it. Blend the weld into the parent metal.

questions.q: Why should the cleaned, bare rail be primed on the same day?
o: Primer helps the welds set harder as they cool down
Bare steel soon rusts in humid air, and rust spoils paint
Primer must go on while the steel is still warm from grinding
The customer can then see that the job is nearly finished
questions.why: In Jamaica's humid air, bare steel starts to rust within hours. Priming promptly protects it and gives the top coat a sound surface to stick to.

questions.q: A drawing gives a length of 750 ±1.5 mm. Which measured length fails?
questions.why: 750 ±1.5 allows 748.5 mm to 751.5 mm. 751.8 mm is 0.3 mm over the largest size allowed, so it fails.

questions.q: Ricardo marks five holes 150 mm apart, measuring each from the one before, and his reading is 0.5 mm long each time. How far out is the fifth hole?
o: 0.5 mm
1.0 mm
2.0 mm
2.5 mm
questions.why: There are four spaces between five holes, so the error adds up to 4 × 0.5 = 2.0 mm. Measuring every hole from one datum would keep each within 0.5 mm.

questions.q: The practical frame is 900 mm × 600 mm. About what should each diagonal read when it is square?
questions.why: Diagonal = √(900² + 600²) = √1 170 000, which is about 1 082 mm. It is not a 3-4-5 triangle, so work it out with Pythagoras.
